openingMessage: The price of success is hard work, dedication to the job at hand, and the determination that whether we win or lose, we have applied the best of ourselves to the task.
openingWhy: Some days the well wins anyway — weather, downhole, plain luck. What can't ever happen is the well winning because we showed up loose. Rained out and rescheduled with the standard intact is a good day. Finished early with steps skipped is a loss, whatever the ticket says.
leadershipThought: Recognition is culture in action. When you name what someone did right, you tell the whole crew what right looks like. Kudos to the ones doing it right every day.

Stop Work Authority Exercised — Unsafe Man Basket Operations (Line of Fire)
Man basket work is one of the highest-risk lift operations on an oil and gas site — Stop Work Authority before elevation is always the right call when anything about the setup looks wrong.

Positive Observation — LOTO Disconnect Completed Efficiently (Energy Isolation)
LOTO, atmospheric testing, and hold points together form a complete energy control system — don't shortcut any one of them, even on a quick job.

Stop Work by Equipment Operator — Spotter Lost Visual (Mobile Equipment)
Equipment operators own Stop Work Authority too — stop the moment you lose your spotter; regaining visual contact is the only acceptable restart condition.

Crane Work — Horse Head Installation and Flowline Connection (Mobile Equipment)
Crane work demands real-time stop work authority — if anything changes during the lift, the person on the ground is empowered to call the stop immediately.

specialFocus.title: Who Are We? — Have Your Teammate's Six
specialFocus.why:
This one comes from the top. Today I — Mike Lyons — took a call from a company man. Not about our monitors. Not about our paperwork. About camaraderie: he thought there should be more of it among our team. That call should never have to happen, and here is why. Who are we? We are the first ones on location and the last ones to leave. We are AGT and safety oversight — the second set of eyes that ops counts on. Acting as an individual when your job is done — not having the common courtesy to ask the teammates around you if they need a hand — is turning your back on this organization. And turning your back on this organization is turning your back on your teammates within it. I want people around me who have my back the way a SEAL team has each other's: you would never not cover your brother. You have his six. That is the team I'm building, and every one of you is in it.

And this is not a weird ask — answer it honestly: what kind of partner do you want supporting you in times of duty? The first name that comes to your mind — that part is easy. Then notice how fast the list drops off after it. Your goal as a person within this group is to be that first name. Be someone people can count on. And if you can't be counted on — if you don't want to help others first — then you don't belong here. You're in the way of the people who do.
standard: When your task is done, you are not done. Find your teammates on location and say it out loud: “I'm here to help — what can I do?” Every location, every time.
Out of the truck, clear-minded, involved. You cannot be a second set of eyes for ops from the cab. First to location, last to leave means present the whole way through — eyes up, in the work.
Cover your teammate's six. Nobody wearing Canon on their chest works alone while another Canon hand watches from a distance. If one of us is still working, all of us are still working.
specialFocus.scenario: Two Canon techs on the same pad. One finishes his monitor setup, checks his box, and walks back to the truck. Fifty yards away, his teammate is still setting up alone in the heat. The company man sees all of it — and what he sees isn't laziness. It's two individuals wearing the same logo instead of one team. Now run it the other way: the first tech finishes, walks over, and says 'I'm done — what do you need?' Same two people, same job. But now the work goes faster, the location is safer because there's a second set of eyes on the task, and what the client remembers is a crew that covers each other. One of those crews gets called back by name. The other gets a phone call made about them. We got that phone call today. There will not be a second one.
questions: What kind of partner do you want supporting you in times of duty? A name came to mind instantly — why that name? What are they doing that you're not? And the harder question: whose first-name list are YOU on?
When your part of the job is done, what is the very next thing you do — honestly? Do you walk toward your teammate, or toward your truck?
What does having someone's six actually look like on a location? Give me a real example from this week — who covered you, or who did you cover?
If a company man watched only you for an entire shift, would he describe you as 'here to help' or 'here to do a task'? What exactly would he see?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: First to location. Last to leave. Out of the truck and involved. And before you head for the gate, you ask every teammate still working: 'What can I do?' You never leave a brother or sister working alone — you have their six. That is who we are.
